prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Traffic facility poles: When traffic management facilities such as traffic signal lights, traffic monitoring poles, and traffic sign boards are arranged in the median/side median, they shall be aligned with the centerline of streetlights and other facilities within the median. Where there is no side median or central median, traffic signal lights, traffic monitoring poles, and traffic sign boards shall be arranged within the sidewalk facility zone and shall not occupy or obstruct sidewalk passage or the area adjacent to pedestrian crosswalk lines. Traffic facility poles should, as far as possible, achieve “one pole for multiple uses.” When streetlight poles and sign poles are combined into one pole, full consideration shall be given to the issue of traffic signs being obscured by the light below (“lamp-shadow blindness”), and the relationship among various poles and roadside trees shall be coordinated comprehensively to avoid roadside trees obstructing signs, monitoring devices, and traffic signal lights. 2. Central median guardrails and side median guardrails: Their layout should start from the stop line at intersections and shall not hinder normal vehicle movement. End warning signs shall be set at the starting point, and reflectors, reflective film, etc. shall be installed on the posts. The length and height of each guardrail panel shall take into account functional requirements, manufacturing process, and the requirements of the deployment area. Figure 4.3-1 Example of Central Median Guardrail 3. Pedestrian guardrails shall start from the end position of the sidewalk curb ramp and be laid close to the inner edge line of the curb. For guardrails at locations with fall hazards, the clear spacing of vertical members shall not be greater than 0.11 m, and structures with footholds are not recommended. Pedestrian guardrails that are not fully isolating or serve a warning function may adopt a post-and-chain form. 4. Selected Indicators:

 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.

Sidewalks shall be firm and level, with no cracks, missing bricks, damage, or other defects; joint widths shall be uniform and joints fully filled. All manhole covers shall be flush with the sidewalk elevation and in good condition, and their strength must meet sidewalk traffic requirements. 2. Sidewalks must have a base course and bedding course of sufficient strength. For settlement, breakage, or damage caused by insufficient base-course strength, the base course shall first be reinforced before the surface blocks are repaved. 3. To ensure safe pedestrian passage in rain and snow, the longitudinal slope of sidewalk ramps shall be ≤1:20. Smooth-surfaced ramp slabs shall be treated with anti-slip measures. Ramps that do not meet the requirements shall be demolished and reconstructed during rectification. 1.2 At-Grade Crossing System 1.2.1 Crossing at At-Grade Intersections 1. Basic Principles A. The slow-traffic organization for pedestrians and non-motor vehicles within grade-separated interchange areas shall be continuous, safe, and convenient, and should be arranged at ground level to avoid pedestrians and non-motor vehicles having to go up and down or increasing detour distances. 2. Quality Enhancement A. Reducing crossing distance Reducing the curb radius at intersections can effectively lower turning speeds, shorten pedestrian crossing distances, and enlarge pedestrian waiting areas. The facility strip or green belt along the roadside may also be appropriately used to create a pedestrian stopping space. Secondary crossing refuge island When the pedestrian or bicycle crossing traverses more than 4 lanes of two-way motor vehicle traffic, or when the crossing length exceeds 16 m, a secondary crossing refuge island shall be set in the center of the road. The island width shall not be less than 2 m, and in difficult circumstances not less than 1.5 m. On roads with a median strip (or where lane width can be reduced), pedestrian crossings on signal-free sections shall be provided with a “Z”-shaped secondary crossing refuge island. This not only improves pedestrian crossing efficiency, but also prevents interference between pedestrians and motor vehicles. D. For systems that are severely damaged or can no longer operate normally, reconstruction shall be carried out according to actual needs. 4.3 Urban Furniture 4.3.1 Traffic Management Facilities The color, form, style, and other aspects of traffic management facilities in the same city should be as unified as possible; roads in certain special areas may be designed with appropriate distinctive features. 1. Traffic facility poles: When traffic management facilities such as traffic signal lights, traffic monitoring poles, and traffic sign boards are arranged in the median/side median, they shall be aligned with the centerline of streetlights and other facilities within the median. Where there is no side median or central median, traffic signal lights, traffic monitoring poles, and traffic sign boards shall be arranged within the sidewalk facility zone and shall not occupy or obstruct sidewalk passage or the area adjacent to pedestrian crosswalk lines. Traffic facility poles should, as far as possible, achieve “one pole for multiple uses.” When streetlight poles and sign poles are combined into one pole, full consideration shall be given to the issue of traffic signs being obscured by the light below (“lamp-shadow blindness”), and the relationship among various poles and roadside trees shall be coordinated comprehensively to avoid roadside trees obstructing signs, monitoring devices, and traffic signal lights. 2. Central median guardrails and side median guardrails: Their layout should start from the stop line at intersections and shall not hinder normal vehicle movement. End warning signs shall be set at the starting point, and reflectors, reflective film, etc. shall be installed on the posts. The length and height of each guardrail panel shall take into account functional requirements, manufacturing process, and the requirements of the deployment area. Figure 4.3-1 Example of Central Median Guardrail 3. Pedestrian guardrails shall start from the end position of the sidewalk curb ramp and be laid close to the inner edge line of the curb. For guardrails at locations with fall hazards, the clear spacing of vertical members shall not be greater than 0.11 m, and structures with footholds are not recommended. Pedestrian guardrails that are not fully isolating or serve a warning function may adopt a post-and-chain form. 4. Vehicle-stopping bollards / vehicle-blocking stones: Materials shall be selected according to the location and functional requirements, using durable materials such as stone, cast iron, stainless steel, galvanized steel, or aluminum alloy. The spacing between bollards should be 1.3 m–1.5 m, and the height should be 0.4 m–0.6 m. Reflective film, warning lights, etc. shall be installed. 151 Figure 4.3-2 Example of Vehicle-Stopping Bollards / Vehicle-Blocking Stones 5.
